title: Sport and Society
description: Ten texts about sport and the communities around it: a small-town football Friday, the growth of women's soccer, a Paralympic swimmer, pressure in youth sports, the cost of a new stadium, a marathon volunteer, a neighborhood basketball court, a sports museum, a referee and a team chef.

lessons.title: Friday Night in Millbrook
lessons.summary: A newcomer describes how a small town comes together for its high school football game.
lessons.text:
In Millbrook, a town of about 6,000 people, Friday night in the fall belongs to football. Traditionally, the stores on Main Street close early, and almost everyone walks or drives to the field behind the high school. I moved here three years ago, and I still find it remarkable how completely one game can unite a whole town.

The team is called the Panthers. A black panther is painted at the center of the field, and a boy in a panther costume waves at the children. Nobody in Millbrook has ever seen a real panther, as far as I know, but everybody owns at least one shirt with a panther on it.

By October, the evenings are cold. At the last game of the season, there was frost on the grass before the first quarter ended, and the players' breath rose like smoke under the lights. The frost made the field shine, and the families in the stands wrapped themselves in blankets and drank hot chocolate.

Food is part of the ritual. The parents' club sells fried chicken, fried potatoes and bags of roasted peanuts, and the money pays for the team's travel. By the end of the night, the ground under the stands is covered with peanut shells.

Then there is the band. What I love most is the brass section: twelve students whose brass instruments shine like gold under the lights. At halftime, they march onto the field and play old songs, and the older fans sing along.

Not everyone sees the game in the same way, of course. Football is a sport of collisions, and some parents have begun to worry about what those collisions do to a teenager's head. Last year, the school bought new helmets and changed its rules so that players hit each other less often in practice. Most people I spoke to thought this was a wise change; a few thought it was not enough. Both groups still came to the games.

This year the Panthers did not win many games, but the final game was spectacular. With ten seconds left, a quiet student named Danny Ruiz caught a long pass and ran all the way to the end of the field to score. The stands exploded. Strangers hugged, and the players raised their fists toward the crowd. I saw a grandmother and a little boy bump fists, both of them crying with joy.

Most people will forget the score in a year or two. The feeling, I suspect, will stay. On a cold Friday, a whole town stood together for two hours, and that, more than any spectacular play, is what unites Millbrook.

Questions:
What traditionally happens in Millbrook on Friday nights in the fall?
The stores close early, and almost everyone goes to watch the high school football game.
What is the team called, and what is painted on the field?
The team is called the Panthers, and a black panther is painted at the center of the field.
What does the parents' club sell, and why?
It sells fried chicken, fried potatoes and peanuts, and the money pays for the team's travel.
Why do some parents worry about football?
They worry about what the collisions do to a teenager's head.
What did the school do about it?
It bought new helmets and changed its rules so that players hit each other less often in practice.
Why was the final game spectacular?
With ten seconds left, Danny Ruiz caught a long pass and ran all the way to score.

lessons.title: The Growth of Women's Soccer
lessons.summary: A short report on how women's soccer grew from a small sport into a professional game, and what it still lacks.
lessons.text:
Not long ago, a girl who loved soccer had almost no chance of being paid to play it. Today, professional women's teams fill stadiums and appear on national television. How did such a change happen, and how far does it still have to go?

Part of the answer lies in success. The United States national team won the first Women's World Cup in 1991 and won it again in 1999, when more than 90,000 people watched the final in California. Those victories showed girls that soccer could be their sport, too, and the growth that followed was most pronounced among the youngest players. In many towns, there are now almost as many girls' teams as boys' teams, and the change is even more pronounced in the cities.

Another part of the answer lies in money. For years, professional leagues opened and then closed again. Players had other jobs and traveled to games by bus, sometimes for ten hours. Now most teams travel by airplane and train on proper fields. One player I spoke to remembered her first airplane trip with her team as the moment she finally felt like a professional.

The game itself has changed, too. Coaches study video and plan every match in detail, and the tactical level of a good women's game is now very high. Many of these coaches are women who earned their certification after their own playing careers. A coaching certification takes months of study, and in several countries the national association now pays for former players to complete it.

The question of inclusion remains politically sensitive. Some people argue that women's sport deserves the same pay and attention as men's, while others answer that pay should follow ticket sales and television audiences. Politically, the two sides rarely agree. What both accept is that inclusion begins in childhood: a girl who never gets the chance to play will never become a fan, a coach or a professional.

There have been disappointments along the way. Leagues have collapsed, and some clubs have closed temporarily when the money ran out. A few years ago, one popular club had to leave its stadium temporarily and play its home games at a college field. For its fans, it was a deep disappointment.

Yet the progress is hard to deny. Last spring, two teams met in a regional cup semifinal that was decided on aggregate, which means that they played each other twice and the goals from both games were added together. One of the teams lost the first game 1 to 0 but won the second 2 to 0, so it won the semifinal 2 to 1 on aggregate. More than 15,000 people watched each game, a crowd that would have been hard to imagine twenty years ago.

Questions:
Where was the growth of women's soccer most pronounced?
It was most pronounced among the youngest players and in the cities.
How has the game itself changed?
Coaches plan every match in detail, and the tactical level of a good game is now very high.
What do many former players do after their playing careers?
Many of them earn a coaching certification and become coaches.
Why does the question of inclusion remain politically sensitive?
Some people want the same pay and attention as men's sport, while others think pay should follow ticket sales and audiences.
What disappointment did one popular club's fans experience?
Their club had to leave its stadium temporarily and play its home games at a college field.
What does it mean that a semifinal is decided on aggregate?
It means that the teams play twice and the goals from both games are added together.

lessons.title: Profile: Lena Hart, Swimmer
lessons.summary: A profile of a swimmer with limited use of her legs who went from fearing the pool to racing at the Paralympic Games.
lessons.text:
Lena Hart was nine years old when she first went into a swimming pool, and she did not go in happily. Because of a complication at birth, she has limited mobility in her legs. As a child, she walked with the help of two metal sticks and avoided anything that might make her fall. When her doctor explained the complication to her, he suggested swimming, since water supports the body.

Lena hated the idea. What she remembers most about that first day is how ashamed she felt as she sat at the edge of the pool while other children watched. "I wasn't ashamed of my legs, exactly," she says. "I was ashamed of needing help in front of everyone."

Her mother had promised that she would not have to jump. So, very slowly, Lena waded into the shallow end, holding the wall with both hands. The water came up to her knees, then to her shoulders. "And then something strange happened," she says. "My legs stopped being the problem. For the first time I could remember, I felt light. My mobility in the water was almost normal."

Within a year, she was swimming independently. Her first coach tried to teach her a stroke whose kick is often called a frog kick, because you pull your legs up and push them out and back, the way a frog does. Lena could not do it. "I looked less like a frog and more like a sinking boat," she says, laughing. Instead, she and her coach built a stroke around her arms, and she soon discovered that she was fastest when she swam on her back.

At 16, she made a vow: one day, she would swim at the Paralympic Games. She shared the vow only with her mother and her coach, and both took it seriously. Her training became intensive: two hours in the pool before school, an hour in the gym after it, six days a week. Intensive training, she admits, has a cost. She missed parties, and on some dark winter mornings she cried in the car on the way to the pool.

Today, at twenty-four, Lena has competed at two Paralympic Games and kept her vow twice over. She is studying to become a physical therapist, and she lives independently in a small apartment near her training pool. She no longer feels ashamed of her metal sticks, which she leaves at the edge of the pool before every race.

When young people ask her for advice, she always gives them the same answer. "You don't have to be brave," she tells them. "You just have to wade in, a little at a time." If she had refused to wade into the water on that first day, she says, she would not be the person she is now.

Questions:
Why does Lena have limited mobility in her legs?
She has limited mobility because of a complication at birth.
Why was she ashamed on her first day at the pool?
She was ashamed of needing help in front of everyone.
How did she get into the water?
She waded slowly into the shallow end, holding the wall with both hands.
What could she not do in the pool?
She could not do the frog kick, so she built a stroke around her arms.
What vow did she make at 16?
She vowed that one day she would swim at the Paralympic Games.
What advice does she give young people?
She tells them that they don't have to be brave; they just have to wade in, a little at a time.

lessons.title: How Much Is Too Much?
lessons.summary: An essay weighing the benefits and the dangers of serious sport for children.
lessons.text:
Every weekend, millions of children play organized sports, and every weekend, somewhere, a parent shouts too loudly from the side of a field. Has youth sport become too serious, or are such worries exaggerated? As with most questions about children, the honest answer is that both sides have a point.

Consider first the case for serious youth sport. Children who train regularly learn discipline, teamwork and how to lose without falling apart. Good coaches instruct children not only in skills but also in habits: arriving on time, listening, and helping a teammate who is struggling. A child who joins a club at the intermediate level and slowly works her way up to the top team learns something about effort that no classroom can teach. Seen this way, high expectations are not cruel; they are a form of respect.

There is also a practical argument. In many sports, children who start late are at a real disadvantage, because the others already have years of practice behind them. Parents who push their children to train more are presumably trying to protect them from that disadvantage, and it would be unfair to call every such parent ignorant or selfish.

Now consider the other side. Children's bodies are still growing, and doctors warn that playing one sport all year, without adequate rest, can lead to injuries that were once seen only in adults. Adequate rest is not laziness; it is part of training. Moreover, many children who quit sport give a simple reason: it stopped being fun. Not only do they lose the exercise, but they often lose the friendships that came with it.

Much of the pressure also rests on an illusion. Many parents believe that enough training will turn their child into a professional, or at least win a place at a good college. In reality, only a tiny number of young athletes ever reach that level, and a parent who builds a family's whole life around the illusion may simply be ignorant of how small the chances are.

So what would a rational approach look like? It would probably begin by asking the child what he or she actually wants. A rational parent might also minimize the things that make sport stressful: the long trips to faraway games, the expensive private lessons, the anxious analysis of every game on the drive home. Clubs can minimize pressure, too. Some now instruct their coaches to give every child real playing time, especially at the intermediate level, where most children will presumably stay.

What children seem to need, in the end, is neither total freedom nor total pressure. They need adults who take their sport seriously without taking it over. If more parents remembered why they themselves loved playing as children, fewer children would be quitting today.

Questions:
What do good coaches instruct children in?
They instruct children in skills and also in habits, such as arriving on time and helping a teammate.
Why are children who start late at a disadvantage?
They are at a disadvantage because the others already have years of practice behind them.
Why is adequate rest important?
Without adequate rest, children can get injuries that were once seen only in adults.
What illusion do many parents believe in?
They believe that enough training will turn their child into a professional.
What might a rational parent minimize?
A rational parent might minimize long trips, expensive lessons and the anxious analysis of every game.
What do children seem to need, in the end?
They need adults who take their sport seriously without taking it over.

lessons.title: Who Pays for the Stadium?
lessons.summary: An essay on the arguments for and against a city helping to pay for a new baseball stadium.
lessons.text:
Last year, the city of Harbor Point voted on whether to help pay for a new stadium for its baseball team. The team's owners promised jobs, visitors and pride. Their critics promised debt. Now that the stadium is half built, it is worth asking what the arguments on each side really were.

The case for the stadium rested on projections. According to the team's projections, the stadium would bring two million visitors a year, create 1,500 jobs and attract new restaurants and hotels to a neglected part of downtown. Taxes on tickets, food and hotel rooms, the owners argued, would offset the city's share of the cost within twenty years. Supporters added that a team gives a city an identity, which cannot be measured in money.

The case against the stadium was just as clear. Economists who study stadiums have found that they rarely produce the growth that their projections promise. Most of the money that fans spend at a game, they point out, would otherwise have been spent somewhere else in the same city. Only a fraction of it is truly new money, and that fraction is usually too small to offset the public cost. Critics also noted that the median household in Harbor Point earns about $48,000 a year, and they asked why families with a median income should help pay for a business owned by some of the richest people in the state.

The debate soon became heated. Protesters gathered outside city hall every week. Some protesters carried signs comparing the cost of the stadium with the city's shortage of teachers; others pointed to a shortage of affordable housing. One of the team's owners allegedly told a member of the city council that the team would move to another city if the vote failed. He allegedly made the remark at a private dinner, but it was never proven that he had said it.

In the end, the two sides reached a compromise. The agreement specified that the team would pay two thirds of the cost and that the city's share could not rise, even if the project went over budget. It also specified that a small fraction of every ticket would go into a fund for youth sports. To pay its share, the city decided to consolidate several old loans into a single cheaper one, and to consolidate two of its offices to save money.

The voters gave their verdict in November: 54 percent in favor. Whether that verdict was wise, nobody can say yet. If the stadium brings the promised life to downtown, it will be remembered as a bold decision; if it does not, the city will still be paying for it long after the last game is played.

Questions:
What did the team's projections promise?
They promised two million visitors a year, 1,500 jobs and new restaurants and hotels downtown.
How would the city's share of the cost be offset, according to the owners?
It would be offset by taxes on tickets, food and hotel rooms.
Why do economists doubt such projections?
Only a fraction of the money fans spend is truly new money, because most of it would be spent in the city anyway.
What did some protesters compare the cost of the stadium with?
They compared it with the city's shortage of teachers and of affordable housing.
What was specified in the agreement?
It specified that the team would pay two thirds of the cost and that the city's share could not rise.
What was the voters' verdict?
They voted 54 percent in favor of the stadium.

lessons.title: A Morning at Mile 13
lessons.summary: A first-time volunteer describes a morning at a marathon water station.
lessons.text:
Sunday evening

Today I volunteered at the city marathon for the first time. I was placed at the water station at mile 13, which is almost exactly halfway, since a marathon is a little over 26 miles long. We had been told that the halfway point is where many runners first begin to suffer, and it was true.

We arrived at 6 in the morning, in the dark. Our station stood in front of the old stone abbey on the hill, and the monks who live in the abbey came out with a table of their own and handed out slices of orange, as they apparently do every year. Our team leader, Gloria, instructed us to fill the paper cups only halfway, so that they would not spill, and to hold them out so that runners could take them without stopping.

At 7:30, far away, we heard the starting pistol. It was a small, sharp sound, but everyone at our station cheered when the pistol went off, even though the runners would not reach us for another hour.

The fastest runners arrived first, calm and silent. Then came the main crowd, thousands of people, and for two hours we could barely distribute the water fast enough. My job was to distribute cups of water, while the girl next to me distributed cups of a sports drink. Our hands were wet and freezing, but nobody complained.

What I had not expected was how many different stories would pass us. Two sisters ran holding hands. One woman stopped beside me, bent over with a stitch in her side, and asked how much farther she had to go. "You're halfway," I told her, and she laughed and said that was the worst news she had heard all day. After a minute, the stitch went away, and she ran on.

Many runners had sore heels, and a nurse at our station spent the morning taking care of heels and toes. Faces were flushed red with effort, even in the cold. One older runner, very flushed and breathing hard, sat down at the side of the road. We gave him water and a banana and waited for him to revive. After ten minutes, he did revive; he stood up, thanked us and kept going.

When the last runners had passed, we packed everything up. The water and fruit that were left were donated to a shelter in town, along with hundreds of thermal blankets that a local company had donated for the finish line. A thermal blanket looks like a thin sheet of silver paper, but it keeps a tired body warm.

I came home cold, wet and very happy. Next year I will volunteer again, or perhaps, if I start training now, I will run.

Questions:
Why is mile 13 called the halfway point?
It is called the halfway point because a marathon is a little over 26 miles long.
What did the monks from the abbey do?
They came out with a table and handed out slices of orange.
What did the writer distribute?
The writer distributed cups of water to the runners.
What happened to the woman with a stitch in her side?
She stopped and rested for a minute, and when the stitch went away, she ran on.
How did the volunteers help the older runner revive?
They gave him water and a banana and waited until he felt better.
What happened to the thermal blankets?
They were donated to a shelter in town, along with the water and fruit.

lessons.title: The Court on Fourth Street
lessons.summary: A coach and his neighbors turn an empty lot into a basketball court for the children of the area.
lessons.text:
For as long as anyone could remember, the empty lot on Fourth Street had been a place that people avoided. Weeds grew through the broken concrete, the only street light had stopped working years before, and at night the lot was truly creepy. Parents told their children to cross the street rather than walk past it.

Then Marcus Bell, who coaches basketball at the middle school, had an idea. The children of the area had nowhere to play; the nearest public court was two miles away, and few families had time to drive there. A court on Fourth Street, he thought, would be a matter of simple convenience: close enough for children to walk to after school.

The first step was to find the owner. The lot belonged to a landlord named Helen Park, who owns several apartment buildings in the area. Marcus expected the landlord to refuse, but she listened to his plan and agreed to rent the lot to the community for a buck a year. "A buck a year," she said, smiling, "and an invitation to the first game."

Next came expertise. Marcus knew basketball, but he knew nothing about building. So he asked for help. A retired builder offered her expertise on the concrete, and an electrical engineer explained that the new lights would need a higher voltage than the old street light could provide. Getting the right voltage meant laying a new cable from the main street, which the city agreed to pay for.

Volunteers did the rest. On a Saturday in May, forty people arrived with gloves and tools. They pulled weeds, cleared away trash and painted lines. The youngest children, too small for real work, sat in a row in matching shirts and looked adorable. A newspaper photographer took a picture of three adorable little boys pretending to throw a ball through the new basket, and it appeared on the front page the next morning.

The court opened in June. To celebrate, Marcus organized a tournament for 16 teams and drew the bracket on a large board by the fence. Each team that wanted to enter put a dollar into a jar, and the money paid for new nets. After every game, children ran to the board to see who had moved up the bracket.

Today, the lot on Fourth Street is the busiest place in the area. The lights stay on until ten, and the sound of bouncing balls has replaced the silence that once made the place so creepy. Parents enjoy the convenience as much as their children do. Not only did the court give the children somewhere to go, but it also gave their parents a reason to talk to one another.

Questions:
Why did people avoid the lot on Fourth Street?
Weeds grew through the concrete, the street light did not work, and at night the lot was creepy.
Why did Marcus think a court there would be a convenience?
It would be close enough for children to walk to after school.
How much did the landlord ask for the lot?
She agreed to rent it to the community for a buck a year.
What did the electrical engineer explain?
He explained that the new lights would need a higher voltage than the old street light could provide.
Why was the photo in the newspaper adorable?
It showed three little boys pretending to throw a ball through the new basket.
How did Marcus organize the tournament?
He drew a bracket for 16 teams on a large board by the fence.

lessons.title: Review: The City Sports Museum
lessons.summary: A review of a new sports museum, praising its interactive rooms and its final film but noting a few weak points.
lessons.text:
The new City Sports Museum opened in April on a narrow peninsula that reaches out into the lake, and its location is part of its charm: from almost every window, visitors see water. Getting to the peninsula takes a short walk across a bridge from the parking lot, and on a sunny day the walk alone is worth the trip.

The building shows its ambitions at once. The entrance hall has a marble floor and, in the middle, a tall marble statue of Nike, the Greek goddess of victory. The ancient Greeks often showed the goddess with wings, ready to crown the winners of races and games; today, of course, her name is better known from a brand of running shoes. The statue is a copy, but a beautiful one.

From the hall, a glass elevator takes visitors to the top floor, and the tour then leads downward through the history of sport. The elevator is slow, and on busy afternoons there is a line. Families with small children have no other way up, so everyone else might consider the stairs.

What sets this museum apart is its technological ambition. Instead of static displays of old shirts and trophies behind glass, most of the rooms are interactive. In one room, visitors can try to return a tennis serve that comes at full speed from a machine; in another, they can test their reaction time against that of a professional runner. My eleven-year-old nephew would happily have spent the whole day in the interactive rooms. The few static displays that remain are well chosen. A row of baseball gloves illustrates how the glove has grown over 150 years, and a wall of running shoes illustrates how technological progress has made them lighter.

Not every room succeeds, however. The section on the history of women's sport is far too small for such an important subject, and two of the technological exhibits were out of order during my visit. The cafe, too, is expensive for what it offers.

The finale nearly makes up for everything. The tour ends in a small round theater where a fifteen-minute film shows great moments from a century of sport, with music played by the city's orchestra. As the orchestra builds toward the finale of the music, the screen fills with athletes crossing finish lines, and then a curtain opens on a wide window over the lake. Around me in the dark, several adults were quietly wiping their eyes.

In short, the museum is a delight, especially for families. Go on a weekday morning if you can, take the stairs instead of the elevator, and save some time for the walk back across the peninsula.

Questions:
Where does the museum stand?
It stands on a narrow peninsula that reaches out into the lake.
What is in the middle of the entrance hall?
There is a marble statue of Nike, the Greek goddess of victory.
How are most of the rooms different from static displays?
Most of the rooms are interactive, so visitors can try things themselves.
What does the row of baseball gloves illustrate?
It illustrates how the glove has grown over 150 years.
What weak points does the reviewer mention?
The section on women's sport is too small, two exhibits were out of order, and the cafe is expensive.
What happens during the finale?
A film shows great moments from sport, with music by the city's orchestra, and then a curtain opens on a window over the lake.

lessons.title: In the Middle: A Referee Speaks
lessons.summary: An interview with an experienced soccer referee about angry fans, instinct, teamwork and mistakes.
lessons.text:
Carla Mendes has been a soccer official at high school and college games for twenty-two years. We met at a cafe near the field where she had just finished working at a youth game.

Why do you do it at all?

Because I love the game, and the game cannot happen without someone in the middle. People forget that. Every Saturday, thousands of children can play because somebody agreed to stand in the rain.

Officials are often treated badly by fans. How do you deal with that?

Most fans are fine. They shout, but they shout at everyone. Real hatred is rare, although I have felt it a few times, usually from adults at children's games, strangely enough. That kind of hatred is hard to forget. I can tolerate a lot of noise. What I will not tolerate is abuse of my assistants or of young players. When someone crosses that line, I stop the game and ask the coach to deal with it.

Is it true that you have a personal rule for every game?

Yup. My doctrine, if you want to call it that, is very simple: be in the right place, stay calm, and never make a decision while you are angry. Every official develops a doctrine like that over the years. Mine just happens to be short.

How much of the job is instinct?

More than people think. You train your instinct by watching thousands of situations, until it tells you what is about to happen before it happens. But instinct has to be checked by the rational part of your mind. The rational part asks: did I actually see contact, or did I only expect it?

You work with two assistants. How do you stay in sync?

We talk before every game and agree on signals. During the game, we use small radios and eye contact. When a team of three officials is in sync, the players hardly notice us, which is exactly the goal. When we are not in sync, everyone notices.

Have you ever made a mistake that you still think about?

Yup. Years ago, I gave a penalty in a college semifinal, and the video later showed that I was wrong. I was so embarrassed that I could not sleep. The next week, I called the coach of the losing team and apologized. He was surprised, but he thanked me. Being embarrassed is part of the job; what matters is what you do next.

What would you say to someone who is thinking about becoming a referee?

Do it. There is a shortage of officials almost everywhere, especially at the youth level. You will be shouted at, of course. But you will also see the best of people, and you will never watch the game in the same way again.

Questions:
Why does Carla do the job?
She loves the game, and the game cannot happen without someone in the middle.
What will Carla not tolerate?
She will not tolerate abuse of her assistants or of young players.
What is her personal doctrine?
Her doctrine is to be in the right place, stay calm and never make a decision while she is angry.
Why must instinct be checked by the rational mind?
The rational mind asks whether she actually saw contact or only expected it.
How do the three officials stay in sync?
They agree on signals before the game and use small radios and eye contact during it.
Why was she embarrassed after a college semifinal?
The video showed that a penalty she had given was wrong.

lessons.title: Feeding the Team
lessons.summary: A profile of a professional hockey team's chef and what he cooks for the players.
lessons.text:
When people imagine the life of a professional athlete, they think of training, travel and fame. They rarely think of lunch. Yet for Tom Becker, head chef of a professional hockey team, lunch is the whole job, along with breakfast and dinner.

Tom arrives at the team's kitchen at 5 in the morning. The first hours are devoted to prep: washing, peeling and cutting the vegetables, fruit and meat for the day. "Prep is the part nobody sees," he says, "but if the prep is wrong, everything is wrong." He chops onions, peppers and herbs by hand, faster than most people could with a machine. When he teaches young cooks to chop, he shows them how to curl the fingers of the hand that holds the food, so that the knife can only touch the knuckles, never the fingertips. "Curl your fingers, and you'll keep them," he tells every new cook.

He does use machines, of course. A large food processor turns fruit, milk and yogurt into the thick drinks that the players have after training. On a busy day, the processor runs for hours, and Tom keeps a second processor in case the first one breaks.

The menu is planned with the team's doctors. Before a game, the players need energy that lasts, so Tom serves pasta, rice and lean meat: grilled chicken, a little steak or pork with roasted vegetables. After a game, he serves more protein to help tired muscles recover. The players' favorite, he admits, is his slow-cooked ribs on Sunday, although he serves ribs only once a week because they are heavy. Steak night is Wednesday, and nobody is ever late for it.

Some changes have been small but meaningful. Two years ago, the kitchen stopped using plastic straws and switched to paper ones. A few players complained that the paper straws went soft in their thick drinks, so Tom found a stronger kind. Food waste is measured carefully, too, and leftover meals are given to a shelter.

What Tom values most, however, is his relationship with the players. Many of them are young, far from home and unused to cooking for themselves. In the summer, he teaches them to cook simple meals: eggs with vegetables, a pork chop with rice, or a pan of fish and potatoes. "If they leave this team knowing how to cook five healthy meals," he says, "I've done my job."

His proudest moment came when the team won the championship three years ago. In the locker room, the players poured champagne over each other, and then over their chef. "I was standing there in my white jacket, covered in champagne," he remembers, smiling. "It was a waste of good champagne, but I have never been happier."

Questions:
What does Tom do in the first hours of the day?
He does the prep: washing, peeling and cutting the vegetables, fruit and meat.
Why does he teach young cooks to curl their fingers?
If they curl their fingers, the knife can only touch the knuckles, never the fingertips.
What does the food processor make?
It turns fruit, milk and yogurt into thick drinks for the players.
What does Tom serve before a game?
He serves pasta, rice and lean meat, such as chicken, a little steak or pork.
Why did the players complain about the paper straws?
They complained because the paper straws went soft in their drinks.
What happened when the team won the championship?
The players poured champagne over each other and over their chef.
